stories.title: James Marcellino Re-Joins Colliers’ New York City Office as Vice President
stories.excerpt: More than 13 years after departing Colliers as an associate director, James Marcellino has returned to the company’s New York office as a vice president. Starting today, Aug. 10, , Marcellino’s new role will focus on office leasing and tenant representation as Colliers continues expanding its New York presence, according to an announcement by the firm. John Gallagher, executive managing director for New York City at Colliers, called Marcellino’s return “another important step” in the firm’s growth. “His institutional ownership experience and entrepreneurial perspective will bring immediate value to our clients and our team, and we’re thrilled to welcome him back,” Gallagher said in a statement. The executive brings with him more than 17 years of experience advising institutional owners, landlords and occupiers on office leasing. In his most recent work as a real estate consultant, Marcellino advised the Bracha Group, Modernus Architectural Products, and Christie’s International Real Estate’s leading residential sales team, the Gottlieb Team. Marcellino previously served as vice president of leasing at L&L Holding Company from 2023 to 2024, according to the announcement. While there, he oversaw leasing strategy for its 6.3 million-square-foot portfolio and completed nearly 344,000 square feet of office and retail transactions. Marcellino first arrived at Colliers as an associate director in late 2011. He departed in 2013 for an associate role at CBRE, and eventually moved on to leasing leadership positions at CIM Group and the Moinian Group. “Colliers has built a tremendous platform in New York, and I’m excited to return at a time when clients are looking for thoughtful, experienced guidance on increasingly complex real estate decisions,” Marcellino said in a statement. “I’ve built my career on strong relationships and finding opportunities that create meaningful value for clients, and I’m excited to continue that work at Colliers.” Marcellino earned his un
bullets: James Marcellino rejoins Colliers NYC as VP after 13-year absence
Focus: office leasing and tenant representation in New York market
Brings 17+ years institutional owner and landlord advisory experience
stories.summary: Colliers has rehired James Marcellino as vice president in its New York office to expand office leasing and tenant representation. Marcellino brings 17+ years advising institutional owners, landlords, and occupiers on office transactions and previously worked at L&L Holding Company. The hire signals Colliers' commitment to growing its NYC brokerage presence.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. This is an office-focused hire and does not signal shifts in rental demand, capital availability, or construction feasibility for apartment development.

stories.title: Westville to Open at 540 Third Avenue in Murray Hill
stories.excerpt: Westville is getting ready to open its 12th location in the U.S. and bring a selection of classic American foods to Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood. The restaurant brand just signed a 4,148-square-foot lease at the base of 540 Third Avenue, also known as the Dian, a 22-story, 160-unit residential building at the corner of Third Avenue and East 36th Street, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. The lease comprises 2,739 square feet on the ground floor and 1,409 square feet on the lower level. The asking rent and the length of the lease were not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in the nearby Herald Square area was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. CBRE’s Robert Bonicoro and Betsy Da Silva represented Westville in the lease, while Meridian’s James Famularo and Jordan Langer represented ownership, which is a joint venture between Gilar Realty and Ranco Capital. CBRE did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. “Westville had its pick of locations in this market, and its decision to commit long-term at 540 Third Avenue underscores the continued demand for well-built, well-located retail on Third Avenue,” Langer said in a statement. Meridian did not disclose when Westville will open its new Murray Hill location. The franchise also has Manhattan restaurants in the West Village, Chelsea, the East Village, the Upper East Side and on Wall Street, as well as a spot in Long Island City, Queens. Westville opened its first location outside of New York City in Northern Virginia. “When Whole Foods and Westville commit to the same few blocks within months of each other, that is not a coincidence, it is a corridor being repositioned in real time,” Famularo said in a statement. “Ownership delivered a first-class space and held firm on value, and we brought in an operator that will draw customers from the day it opens.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserve
bullets: Westville restaurant signs 4,148 SF lease at 540 Third Avenue, Murray Hill
160-unit residential building (the Dian) attracting ground-floor dining anchor tenant
Herald Square retail averaging $394/SF asking rent in Q2 2026
stories.summary: Westville, a classic American restaurant brand, signed a 4,148-square-foot lease at the base of the Dian, a 22-story, 160-unit residential building at Third Avenue and East 36th Street in Manhattan's Murray Hill neighborhood. The space spans 2,739 SF on the ground floor and 1,409 SF on the lower level. The lease reflects continued retail leasing activity and demand for restaurant concepts in the Murray Hill submarket.
stories.impact: Validates retail demand and street-level activation in Murray Hill residential buildings; successful ground-floor lease-up at 540 Third Avenue (owned by Gilar/Ranco) demonstrates mixed-use viability in the area, reducing lease-up risk and NOI pressure for residential developments anchored with quality retail. Signals continued appetite for restaurant concepts in Manhattan multifamily buildings.

stories.title: Mamdani, MTA Look to Proptech Solutions to Cool Subways and Heat Buildings
stories.excerpt: The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) and Mayor Zohran Mamdani are considering high tech options to transfer heat out of subway stations and into the buildings above, in what would likely be a complicated and pricey infrastructure project. Still, city officials and the MTA believe it could be worth it to provide straphangers with a more comfortable wait on platforms, by using the heat generated below to cut energy to commercial and residential buildings above ground. “We are exploring a lot of possible options to make stations more comfortable,” MTA Chairman Janno Lieber said during a Monday press conference in the Chambers Street Station on the J and Z lines. “We’re looking into innovative energy networks called TENs and the geothermal concepts that will allow us to capture, store and then transfer the excessive heat in a subway station so that it can be used come the winter to heat the buildings upstairs.” While the technology has never been used in coordination with a transit system before, some buildings in New York City gather heat from below ground through geothermal technology, including St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Midtown and 555 Greenwich Street in Hudson Square. It is most widely used in Canada and Europe, according to Lieber, and proptech companies have been showcasing the use of geothermal piles as building infrastructure for several years now. It’s unclear what exactly the technology would look like on a grand scale or how many buildings it would serve, but city officials such as New York City Comptroller Mark Levine believe it could get complicated between city, state and private stakeholders. But it could be expanded to cultivate heat from grocery store refrigerators and small data centers scattered across the five boroughs. bullets: MTA and Mayor Mamdani explore thermal energy networks (TENs) to capture subway heat
Technology would transfer excess platform heat to warm buildings above ground
Never before deployed in transit coordination; infrastructure project cost unspecified
stories.summary: New York City officials and the MTA are exploring thermal energy networks (TENs) and geothermal concepts to capture excess heat from subway stations and transfer it to residential and commercial buildings above ground. MTA Chairman Janno Lieber stated the agency is considering this innovation to improve passenger comfort while reducing energy costs for above-ground properties. The technology has not yet been deployed in coordination with a transit system.
stories.impact: Early-stage but potentially game-changing for NYC multifamily economics if deployed at scale: capturing subway waste heat could materially lower operating costs and carbon footprint for residential buildings proximate to major transit, improving NOI and asset values. Watch for pilot projects; any TEN deployment would create a competitive advantage for developments near high-heat subway corridors (e.g., Manhattan core, busy lines). Feasibility and capex remain unproven.

stories.title: Private Equity Firm OceanSound Expands to 32K SF at SL Green’s 450 Park Avenue
stories.excerpt: New York-based private equity group OceanSound Partners has expanded by more than 10,000 square feet at SL Green Realty’s 450 Park Avenue office tower in Midtown. A new five-year lease secured OceanSound 32,032 square feet across the entire eighth, 22nd and 23rd floors of the office tower at the corner of Park Avenue and East 57th Street, according to SL Green. OceanSound previously subleased 21,640 square feet across the 22nd and 23rd floors. Savills’ John Johnson represented OceanSound in the deal, while CBRE’s Paul Amrich, Neil King, Alex D’Amario, Matthew Dichter and Brooke Dewing negotiated on behalf of SL Green. The exact rent terms of the lease were not disclosed, but asking rent in the building was $170 per square foot as of March, Commercial Observer previously reported. SL Green acquired the Midtown building in April 2022 from Oxford Properties and Crown Acquisitions for $445 million. Steven Durels, SL Green’s director of leasing and real property, said in a statement that the landlord’s recent renovation work inside the building has served to attract tenants looking for “upscale amenities at a luxury location.” Investment advisory services firm Steadfast Financial, OceanSound’s downstairs neighbor, is also a tenant on the 20th and 21st floors. Other prominent tenants in the building include Brazilian bank Banco Bradesco, British-American hedge fund Blue Crest Capital Management, alternative credit platform Willow Tree Credit Partners and principal investing firm Garnett Station Partners. The tower’s flashiest tenant, however, resides on the ground floor, where luxury British sports car brand Aston Martin opened its showroom in 2023. Spokespeople for Savills and CBRE did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: OceanSound Partners expands 32,032 SF at SL Green's 450 Park Avenue, Midtown
Five-year lease adds ~10,400 SF to existing 21,640 SF subleased space
Building asking rent ~$170/SF as of March; recent renovations cited as draw
stories.summary: Private equity firm OceanSound Partners expanded its footprint at 450 Park Avenue (SL Green Realty) by signing a new five-year lease for 32,032 SF across floors 8, 22, and 23. OceanSound previously subleased 21,640 SF on floors 22–23, so the deal represents a ~10,400 SF net expansion. SL Green's recent building renovations were cited as key to attracting the tenant at an asking rent of ~$170/SF.
stories.impact: Negligible impact on multifamily development. This is an office lease renewal and expansion; it signals tenant stickiness and modest office demand in Midtown Manhattan, but does not affect apartment supply, demand, or capital flows. No material second-order effects for residential development.

stories.title: What’s Driving CMBS Distress in the Top U.S. Metro Areas
stories.excerpt: Across the 50 largest commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) markets, $45.8 billion of $393.5 billion in outstanding balance is currently distressed, a balance-weighted rate of 11.6 percent, according to CRED iQ data. Minneapolis, Denver and Oklahoma City lead the distress rankings at 55.1 percent, 35.9 percent and 34.1 percent, respectively, each shaped by a handful of very large loans rather than broader weakness, while Salt Lake City sits at zero, and is therefore the cleanest metro in the top 50. Underneath it all, the property type driving distress has shifted. Multifamily distress has more than doubled since February, from 6 percent to 13 percent, while office distress has eased off from 21.2 percent to 16.7 percent. Minneapolis, Denver and Oklahoma City top the list of most distressed metropolitan areas, followed by Portland, Ore. (30.6 percent), Austin (28.7 percent), and a cluster of Midwest metros, specifically Chicago (26.4 percent), Cleveland (23.6 percent) and Milwaukee (23.1 percent), plus San Francisco (21.5 percent). At the other end of the spectrum, Phoenix, Boston, Las Vegas and Orlando, Fla., all sit around 3 percent, with San Diego and Salt Lake City as the most stable large markets at 0.4 percent and zero percent, respectively. Office remains the largest source of cumulative distress at 16.7 percent ($22.5 billion, roughly half of all distressed balance nationally), followed by mixed-use (14.4 percent), multifamily (13 percent), lodging (10.6 percent) and retail (8.8 percent). Industrial is the clear outperformer at just 1 percent. Regionally, the Midwest’s 10 metros average 22.7 percent distress, driven by concentrated issues in Minneapolis, Chicago, St. Louis, Cleveland, Milwaukee and Cincinnati, while the Northeast, West and South all cluster near 10 percent. bullets: $45.8B of $393.5B CMBS distressed (11.6%) across top 50 metros
Multifamily distress doubled Feb–present: 6% to 13%; office distress fell 21.2% to 16.7%
Minneapolis (55.1%), Denver (35.9%), OKC (34.1%), Portland (30.6%), Austin (28.7%) lead distress
stories.summary: Multifamily distress in CMBS portfolios has more than doubled since February, rising from 6 percent to 13 percent, while office distress has declined from 21.2 percent to 16.7 percent across the 50 largest metro areas. Overall, $45.8 billion of $393.5 billion in CMBS outstanding balance is distressed (11.6% balance-weighted rate). Minneapolis, Denver, and Oklahoma City lead distress rankings, followed by Portland, Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco, while Phoenix, Boston, Las Vegas, and Orlando sit near 3 percent.
stories.impact: CRITICAL: Rapid rise in multifamily CMBS distress (doubled in ~6 months) signals stress in previously stable apartment portfolios—likely driven by rate locks expiring into higher SOFR, occupancy softness, and rent growth deceleration in overleveraged assets. This creates acquisition opportunities for well-capitalized developers with strong balance sheets in distressed metros (Minneapolis, Denver, Austin, Portland, Chicago), where lenders are forced to mark down collateral and may accept lower sale prices. Simultaneously, tight capital and higher cost of carry will force weaker sponsors to exit deals or refinance at losses, reducing new supply pipeline in these markets. Watch for forced sales and value-add opportunities; cap rates may remain compressed due to income stress rather than optimism.
